item.title: AWS Adds Enhanced Observability to SageMaker HyperPod for GPU Training
item.description:
AWS Adds Enhanced Observability to SageMaker HyperPod for GPU Training

Amazon has announced enhanced observability capabilities for Amazon SageMaker HyperPod, a new feature designed to help users diagnose GPU training issues more quickly. This update introduces diagnostic and profiling tools for training workloads running on both Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) and Slurm orchestrators.

🧩 How it works

The new observability layer combines automated outlier detection with static diagnostic rules to surface common failure patterns before they impact training performance.

  • Diagnostic Summary: Utilizes Amazon CloudWatch’s DetectGroupOutliers API to compare each GPU in a training job. It flags GPUs that deviate from their peers based on utilization, memory, temperature, power, and SM clock.
  • Static Diagnostic Rules: Evaluate known failure patterns and organize detected issues by type:
    • Hardware: GPU ECC memory errors, XID faults, and accelerator failures.
    • Network: EFA throughput degradation, packet drops, and retransmissions.
    • Throttling: GPU clock throttling due to heat, board, or reliability limits.
    • Overheating: GPU temperatures exceeding configured limits.

⚙️ Key details

Enhanced observability collects telemetry at two distinct levels, with options for metric storage that have been updated to include CloudWatch as a default choice.

Metric Level Inclusion Coverage
Default Metrics Enabled automatically Cluster health, CPU/disk/OS-level usage, GPU utilization and temperature, and per-job resource utilization. Collected every 30 seconds with ~1–2% CPU overhead and 250–300 MB memory usage.
Advanced Metrics Opt-in Full node exporter suite (host-level), all NVIDIA GPU DCGM and AWS Neuron metrics (clock speeds, power, PCIe, errors), and Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) metrics (throughput, drops, retransmissions).

Previously, only Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus was supported for metrics. CloudWatch is now the default, offering lower pricing compared to Prometheus and tighter integration with the SageMaker console through CloudWatch SageMaker Insights. Users can still choose Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus if they standardize on Prometheus and Grafana for observability.

💡 Why it matters

This capability is delivered as an add-on for EKS-orchestrated clusters and as an extension for Slurm-orchestrated clusters. This structure allows users to control who can install or change the observability layer through AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM). The “Enable HyperPod Observability” setting is checked by default.

#AWS #SageMaker #HyperPod #GPU #Observability #CloudWatch

Source: Introducing enhanced infrastructure observability in Amazon SageMaker HyperPod | Amazon Web Services

item.title: Goose database migration tool supports Go functions and out-of-order changes
item.description:
Goose database migration tool supports Go functions and out-of-order changes

Goose is a database migration tool available as both a CLI and a library. It allows developers to manage database schemas by creating incremental SQL changes or Go functions.

🔍 Overview

The tool supports migrations for multiple database systems. It works against Postgres, MySQL, MariaDB, Spanner, SQLite, YDB, ClickHouse, MSSQL, and Vertica.

🧩 How it works

Goose supports specific migration formats and operational features:

  • Go migrations written as plain functions.
  • Embedded migrations.
  • Out-of-order migrations.
  • Seeding data.
  • Environment variable substitution in SQL migrations.

⚙️ Key details

The CLI includes flags for configuring migration behavior. The following table details specific flags and their functions:

Flag Description
-allow-missing Applies missing (out-of-order) migrations
-certfile File path to root CA’s certificates in pem format (only supported on MySQL)
-dir Directory with migration files (default “.”, can be set via GOOSE_MIGRATION_DIR)
-env Load environment variables from file (default .env)
-no-color Disable color output (NO_COLOR env variable supported)
-no-versioning Apply migration commands with no versioning, in file order
-s Use sequential numbering for new migrations
-ssl-cert File path to SSL certificates in pem format (only supported on MySQL)
-ssl-key File path to SSL key in pem format (only supported on MySQL)
-table Migrations table name (default “goose_db_version”)
-timeout Maximum allowed duration for queries to run

🚀 Availability

Goose is available via several installation methods:

  • Go Install: go install github.com/pressly/goose/v3/cmd/goose@latest installs the binary to your $GOPATH/bin directory.
  • Homebrew: Available for macOS users.
  • Docker: A container image is available for linux/amd64 and linux/arm64.
    • The container image has no shell and supports .sql migrations only.
    • The working directory is /migrations.
    • Tags include vX.Y.Z, vX.Y, vX, and latest.
    • Dockerfiles can copy the binary using: COPY --from=ghcr.io/pressly/goose:v3.30.1 /usr/local/bin/goose /usr/local/bin/goose

AWS Launches Generative AI Starter Kit for Amazon EKS

AWS has introduced a comprehensive toolkit for deploying production-ready Generative AI infrastructure on Amazon EKS. This starter kit is designed for teams running self-hosted LLMs and AI workloads on AWS.

🔍 Overview

  • A comprehensive toolkit for deploying production-ready Generative AI infrastructure on Amazon EKS.
  • Includes pre-configured components for AI Gateway (LiteLLM), LLM Serving (vLLM, SGLang, Ollama), Vector Databases, Embedding Models (TEI), Observability (Langfuse, Phoenix), etc.
  • Built for teams running self-hosted LLMs and AI workloads on AWS.

⚙️ Key details

  • Deploy LLM serving engines (vLLM, SGLang, TGI), AI gateways, vector databases, GPU-accelerated inference platforms, and AI agent frameworks on Kubernetes with a single CLI command.
  • The starter kit includes the configurable components and examples from several categories:
    • AI Gateway - LiteLLM, Kong AI Gateway OSS
    • LLM Model - vLLM, SGLang, Ollama
    • Embedding Model - Text Embedding Inference (TEI)
    • Observability (o11y) - Langfuse, Phoenix
    • GUI App - Open WebUI
    • Vector Database - Qdrant, Chroma, Milvus
    • Workflow Automation - n8n
    • AI Agent - OpenClaw
    • MCP Server - FastMCP 2.0
    • AI Agent Framework - Strands Agents, Agno

🚀 Availability

  • Before you begin, ensure you have the following tools installed: AWS CLI, Terraform, Node.js, kubectl, Helm, Docker and Buildx.
  • To quickly set up a demo environment with infrastructure and essential components and examples: ./cli demo-setup.
  • For a more customized setup, you can use the interactive setup command: ./cli interactive-setup.
  • This starter kit supports deploying NVIDIA Dynamo for optimized LLM inference on Amazon EKS.
  • ./cli nvidia-platform monitoring install # Prometheus + Grafana
  • ./cli nvidia-platform gpu-operator install # NVIDIA GPU Operator
  • ./cli nvidia-platform dynamo-platform install # Dynamo CRDs, Operator, etcd, NATS
  • ./cli nvidia-platform dynamo-vllm install # Deploy a model with vLLM

💡 Why it matters

  • This starter kit simplifies the deployment of production-ready Generative AI infrastructure on Amazon EKS, making it easier for teams to run self-hosted LLMs and AI workloads on AWS.
  • The inclusion of various pre-configured components and examples allows for a more customized and efficient setup.
  • The support for NVIDIA Dynamo ensures optimized LLM inference, enhancing the performance of AI workloads.

item.title: Community fork enables local execution of Japanese Government AI GenAI
item.description:
Community fork enables local execution of Japanese Government AI GenAI

A community-driven project has forked the Japanese Digital Agency’s open-source Government AI “GenAI” (Genai) to enable full local operation using local Large Language Models (LLMs) with an OpenAI-compatible API. This unofficial fork addresses the original system’s dependency on cloud infrastructure (AWS, Azure, Google Cloud) by replacing those dependencies with local or open-source alternatives, allowing the software to run in closed network environments such as LGWAN.

🧩 How it works

The project modifies the Digital Agency’s genai-web repository (MIT License) to function in a local environment. To facilitate merging with upstream changes, the majority of modifications are concentrated in the OpenGENAI layer (backend/ and external apps), while the genai-web UI is kept largely unmodified to preserve the original user experience. The original genai-ai-api is not included in the fork; users must obtain it separately from the Digital Agency’s repository if needed.

⚙️ Key details

The fork currently stands at version v0.13.0. Key technical and functional features include:

  • Hardware Flexibility: Compatible with macOS (Apple Silicon) and Linux systems with NVIDIA GPUs (e.g., NVIDIA DGX Spark).
  • Security & Deployment: Production builds use docker-compose.prod.yml with TLS termination on port 443. Closed-network verification uses docker-compose.verify.yml with HTTP on port 80.
  • Storage: Uses SeaweedFS (port 8333), which is not exposed to the host in production. Artifact downloads are handled via a reverse proxy through S3_PUBLIC_ENDPOINT.
  • Core Capabilities: Includes structured RAG, MCP integration, OCR, skills, Web SSH, and PII detection.

📋 Version History

Version Key Developments
v0.13.0 Training, procedure document/audit, and scheduling wizard
v0.12.0 Two-week work, draw.io editing, image generation chat, and per-building model control
v0.11.0 Multi-tenancy, recommended apps, and Markdown editor HTML/PPTX export
v0.10.0 Notebook features (research/organization), Web SSH, and app display editing
v0.9.0 Third implementation wave: Markdown editor and document creation with pluggable generation APIs
v0.8.0 Second implementation wave: Online forms, procedure bundles, application reception, and MCP
v0.7.0 First implementation wave: Document reading/checking, scheduling, and Excel generation
v0.6.0 PII detection, knowledge base pages, large attachment mapreduce, and Dify error classification
v0.5.0 Production static build deployment, multi-model swapping, and SAML authentication hardening
v0.4.0 Structured RAG, knowledge MCP, Dify integration examples, and My Number checking

💡 Why it matters

The project is explicitly an unofficial fork with no relationship to or approval from the Digital Agency. While early releases focused on replacing cloud dependencies with local/OSS components, the project’s philosophy has expanded to support actual municipal usage in closed networks. This allows local governments and organizations to utilize GenAI capabilities for administrative tasks (such as document processing and scheduling) without relying on external cloud services.

item.title: EvalView 0.9.0 introduces offline regression testing for AI agents
item.description:
EvalView 0.9.0 introduces offline regression testing for AI agents

EvalView 0.9.0 has been released, introducing a tool for regression testing AI agents that operates offline without requiring paid API credentials or making paid inference calls. The release focuses on capturing agent behavior to detect regressions in CI pipelines, distinct from observability platforms or metric scoring tools.

🔍 Overview

EvalView is designed to address the gap between passing tests and user experience by snapshotting an agent’s behavior—specifically which tools it calls, in what order, and with what output. It flags any drift from recorded baselines, functioning as a merge-time regression gate. This approach inverts the traditional evaluation model by recording what an agent actually does now and flagging deviations, rather than requiring developers to pre-define assertions, metrics, or rubrics for “good” behavior.

🧩 How it works

The core workflow involves taking a snapshot of the agent’s current behavior. When new behavior is confirmed to be correct, developers can accept it as the new baseline using evalview snapshot, similar to updating snapshots in Jest. The deterministic tool and sequence diff runs offline, meaning it does not require an API key for the regression check. Additional capabilities are opt-in:

  • LLM Judge: Available when output-quality scoring is desired.
  • Semantic Comparison: Embedding-based comparison can be enabled as an opt-in feature.
  • API Usage: EvalView 0.9.0 utilizes the Responses API.

⚙️ Key details

EvalView is compatible with LangGraph, CrewAI, OpenAI, and Anthropic. It is positioned differently from other tools in the ecosystem:

Category Tools Mentioned Function
Observability Langfuse, LangSmith Visibility into agent operations
Metric Scoring promptfoo, DeepEval, Braintrust Scoring based on predefined metrics
Regression Gate EvalView Flags drift from recorded behavior baselines

Many teams utilize one of the observability or scoring tools for visibility alongside EvalView as a strict regression gate. The tool ensures that while unit tests may pass, behavioral regressions are caught before users notice them.

🔒 Telemetry and Privacy

The installed CLI sends anonymous usage events to PostHog when specific tracked commands are executed. These events use a random installation ID and include the EvalView version, command, runtime, CI environment, and aggregate outcomes. The system explicitly excludes prompts, tool arguments, outputs, paths, and repository names from these events. Developers can opt out of telemetry by setting EVALVIEW_TELEMETRY_DISABLED=1 before first use or by running evalview telemetry off.

💡 Why it matters

Traditional evaluation tools often require manual definitions of success criteria. By automating the baseline recording process, EvalView simplifies the regression testing workflow for AI agents. Because the primary diffing process runs offline without paid inference, it offers a cost-effective way to maintain agent reliability in continuous integration environments, with GitHub runner usage billed separately from the tool itself.

Source: hidai25/eval-view

item.title: Gitea Enables Self-Hosted Software Development Across All Go Platforms
item.description:
Gitea Enables Self-Hosted Software Development Across All Go Platforms

Gitea is a self-hosted all-in-one software development service designed to be the easiest, fastest, and most painless way to set up development infrastructure. It integrates Git hosting, code management, and team collaboration into a single platform.

🧩 How it works

Gitea is written in the Go programming language, which allows it to run across all platforms and architectures supported by Go. This includes:

  • Operating Systems: Linux, macOS, FreeBSD, OpenBSD, and Windows.
  • Architectures: x86, amd64, ARM, RISC-V 64, and PowerPC.

The system supports a comprehensive set of development tools, including:

  • Git hosting and code management
  • Code review and issue tracking
  • Project kanban and wiki functionality
  • Team collaboration
  • Package registry and CI/CD (which can reuse GitHub Actions)

⚙️ Key details

The project provides extensive documentation covering installation, administration, usage, and development. Key resources and commands include:

Resource Purpose
./gitea web Starts the server after building from source
./gitea help Displays all available commands
docs/build-source.md Instructions for building from source or creating distribution packages
docs/development.md Guides for setting up local environments, linting, and testing

For developers contributing to the project, the expected workflow is Fork → Patch → Push → Pull Request. Security vulnerabilities must be reported privately to security@gitea.io.

🚀 Availability

Users can access Gitea through several methods:

  • Online Demonstration: demo.gitea.com
  • Free Service: gitea.com offers a free service with a limited number of repositories.
  • Cloud Deployment: A free trial is available at cloud.gitea.com.
  • Container Deployment: The official image is available for Docker, Podman, or other container runtimes on your own server.
  • Community Support: Questions can be directed to the Discord server or the Discourse forum.

The ecosystem includes an official Go SDK, a CLI tool called gt, and an action runner for Gitea Actions. Third-party projects, SDKs, plugins, and themes are listed on the gitea/awesome-gitea repository.

item.title: Kong Gateway introduces AI traffic capabilities and MCP governance
item.description:
Kong Gateway introduces AI traffic capabilities and MCP governance

Kong or Kong Gateway is a cloud-native, platform-agnostic, scalable API, LLM, and MCP Gateway distinguished for its high performance and extensibility via plugins. It provides advanced AI traffic capabilities with multi-LLM support, semantic security, MCP traffic security and analytics, and more.

🔍 Overview

Kong serves as the central layer for orchestrating microservices or conventional API traffic - and agentic LLM and MCP as well - with ease. By providing functionality for proxying, routing, load balancing, health checking, and authentication, it manages traffic across various architectures.

⚙️ Key details

  • Universal LLM API: Routes traffic across multiple providers including OpenAI, Anthropic, GCP Gemini, AWS Bedrock, Azure AI, Databricks, Mistral, and Huggingface.
  • MCP Capabilities: Includes MCP traffic governance, security, observability, and autogeneration from any RESTful API.
  • AI Features: Offers over 60 features such as AI observability, semantic security, caching, and semantic routing.
  • Security and Routing: Supports authentication and authorization via JWT, basic auth, OAuth, and ACLs.
  • Traffic Management: Handles proxying, SSL/TLS termination, and connectivity support for L4 or L7 traffic.
  • Plugins: Includes 60+ plugins for traffic controls, rate limiting, request/response transformations, logging, and monitoring.
Feature Description
Advanced Routing Load balancing and health checking configurable via RESTful admin API or declarative configuration
Deployment Models Supports Declarative Databaseless Deployment and Hybrid Deployment with control plane/data plane separation
Kubernetes Support Runs natively on Kubernetes thanks to its official Kubernetes Ingress Controller
Plugin Hub Showcases Kong Inc. and community-developed plugins like AWS Lambda, Correlation ID, and Response Transformer

🚀 Availability

Kong is available in various distributions depending on the deployment environment. Users can run it in the cloud, on bare metal, or using containers.

  • Cloud: Sign up for a free trial of Kong Konnect to get started with a cloud-hosted solution.
  • Docker: The docker-compose distribution is suggested for easy setup. A docker installation procedure is also available for running the Kong Gateway in DB-less mode.
  • Installation: To start with the Docker distribution, clone the Docker repository and navigate to the compose folder. Use the command $ KONG_DATABASE=postgres docker-compose --profile database up to start the Gateway stack.

Once started, the Gateway is available on localhost with the following ports:

  • 8000: Send traffic to your service via Kong.
  • 8001: Configure Kong using Admin API or via decK.
  • 8002: Access Kong’s management Web UI (Kong Manager).

Kubernetes Mutating Webhook Released for Automated Sidecar Injection

A new Kubernetes mutating webhook has been developed to automate the injection of sidecar containers into pod specifications. This tool simplifies the management of sidecars within a Kubernetes cluster.

🧩 How it works

To trigger an injection, users must add an annotation—defaulting to sidecar-injector.expedia.com/inject—to the target pod specification, including the name of the ConfigMap that defines the sidecar configuration.

⚙️ Key details

  • Sidecar Scope: Applications are limited to accessing sidecars within their own namespaces.
  • Namespace Watching: By default, the webhook monitors all namespaces except kube-system and kube-public.
  • Configurability: Namespace monitoring settings can be adjusted via Helm values.

🚀 Availability

Deployment is supported through two methods:

  • Helm: Files located in deployment/helm.
  • kubectl: Files located in deployment/kubectl.

To use the Helm method, users must add the repository to their Helm repositories. Those interested in contributing to the codebase are encouraged to review the developer documentation for building and testing procedures.

item.title: Langfuse CLI v4 released with new commands and API versioning
item.description:
Langfuse CLI v4 released with new commands and API versioning

Langfuse has released a new CLI tool, @langfuse/cli, which allows users to interact with the Langfuse API directly from the command line. This new release includes updates to command aliases, input handling for complex JSON structures, and specific versioning rules for self-hosted versus cloud deployments.

📦 Package details

  • Package name: @langfuse/cli
  • Executable: langfuse
  • Legacy name: Previously published under langfuse-cli; the new name is recommended for all future use.

⚙️ Configuration and Host Selection

The CLI does not automatically read .env files. Users must manually configure API access and host selection. Host selection follows a specific priority order:

Priority Configuration Method
1 LANGFUSE_BASE_URL
2 LANGFUSE_HOST
3 EU default

To authenticate, users create a project API key pair under Project settings → API Keys.

🧩 Command and Input Features

  • Lossless input: --body-json and --body-file flags provide a lossless input path for nested objects, arrays, unions, and free-form JSON.
  • Pagination: The CLI can fetch every page of a paginated list, supporting both page- and cursor-based endpoints, with a maximum of 1000 items.
  • Aliases: OpenAPI tags and explicit route versions remain accepted aliases (e.g., scores-v3 list for the canonical scores list).
  • Schema: Verbose OpenAPI operationId values are available in api schema --json but are never required as CLI commands.

🌐 Availability and Versioning

  • V3 API Snapshots: Available on self-hosted deployments only.
  • Langfuse Cloud: Supports v4 and up.
  • Backward Compatibility: Users can use an API snapshot compatible with an older self-hosted deployment.

item.title: Databricks launches Genie Migrate for Serverless to automate classic-to-serverless migration
item.description:
Databricks launches Genie Migrate for Serverless to automate classic-to-serverless migration

Databricks has launched Genie Migrate for Serverless in beta, an agent that automates the migration of jobs and notebooks from classic compute to serverless compute. The agent handles configuration translation and presents changes as reviewable diffs, reducing migration from a manual research project to a review-and-approve step.

🔍 Overview

  • Serverless compute in Databricks removes the operational burden of managing infrastructure, automatically handling provisioning, scaling, and optimization.
  • Serverless usage has grown multifold in the past year, with thousands of customers running notebooks and jobs on it.
  • Most teams still have classic fleets they want to migrate to gain cost and operational benefits.
  • Manual migration has been difficult: flipping a job to serverless often produces errors, access-mode incompatibilities, Spark config issues, or missing libraries.

🧩 How it works

  • The agent runs from the /compute migrate slash command inside Genie on any job or notebook.
  • It is fully managed and requires no setup to start scanning.
  • Because Databricks manages it, the agent reads your job config and workload code inside your own workspace.
  • Before any changes, the agent scans your Jobs and Notebooks and marks each workload with its serverless readiness.
  • Once you pick an eligible workload, the agent proposes the changes needed for serverless and presents them for review before anything is written.
  • Nothing is applied until you approve it.
  • Every change, including code rewrites, is presented as a reviewable diff with a side-by-side comparison.
  • If the agent is unsure about something (for example, whether a Spark conf is still needed), it reports the conf rather than removing it.
  • For a larger fleet, you can run Genie Migrate for Serverless in the background with the Databricks CLI.
  • Your original job does not change until you review and approve its migration, and approving keeps the job’s ID, schedule, and permissions.

⚙️ Key details

Aspect Detail
Launch status Beta
Invocation /compute migrate slash command in Genie
Setup required None (fully managed)
Scope Jobs and notebooks inside the workspace
External sources Not supported yet (e.g., Databricks Asset Bundles, Git folders)
Change application Only after explicit approval
Diff presentation Side-by-side comparison of what will change and what will not
Uncertainty handling Reports Spark confs rather than removing them
Validation today Deterministic checks for correctness
Validation coming Deeper runtime validation in isolated sandbox against classic baseline
Fleet migration Background runs via Databricks CLI
Job identity preserved Job ID, schedule, and permissions retained after approval

🚀 Availability

  • Genie Migrate for Serverless is available now in beta.
  • No setup is required; the agent runs from within Genie in your workspace.
  • Background fleet scanning and migration are supported via the Databricks CLI.

💡 Why it matters

  • Moves the translation knowledge from the practitioner’s head and trial-and-error onto the platform.
  • Turns workload migration into a review-and-approve step rather than a research project.
  • Keeps judgment with the user: whether to migrate now, whether proposed changes look right, and whether the migrated run is healthy.
  • Provides an explicit contract (side-by-side diff) that can be handed to a manager or on-call rotation.
  • Is honest about what it has and has not proven, with runtime validation coming to show correctness signals before apply.

#Databricks #Serverless #Migration #Genie #DataEngineering #AI

Source: Introducing Genie Migrate for Serverless

item.title: Using Amazon Bedrock CloudWatch metrics and evals for LLM observability
item.description:
Using Amazon Bedrock CloudWatch metrics and evals for LLM observability

Airbnb uses Amazon Bedrock to run its internal coding agent tool, AirChat, and has developed a specific observability workflow that combines AWS CloudWatch metrics with custom evaluations. This approach allows the engineering team to monitor production performance, manage costs, and validate model changes effectively.

🔍 Overview

Amazon Bedrock provides access to foundation models from multiple providers through a common API, with AWS managing the underlying infrastructure. At Airbnb, thousands of engineers use AirChat weekly to run coding agents. These agents send model requests through an internal LLM gateway that runs on Amazon Bedrock, ensuring that Airbnb’s code, prompts, and model responses are processed within AWS. The system integrates with standard AWS access controls and monitoring tools.

⚙️ Key Details

To manage the impact of frequent model updates, Airbnb utilizes a combination of operational metrics and quality evaluations:

  • Evaluations (Evals): Before a new model rollout, the team runs evals on a fixed set of representative tasks to measure the model’s score and cost per task.
  • Production Observability: After a rollout, observability data is used to compare production usage against eval results. If discrepancies exist, the team investigates the cause.
  • Cost Per Task: This is defined as the list-price cost of all tokens an agent uses to finish one task. It serves as a key metric alongside performance scores to determine default model and reasoning effort settings.

CloudWatch Metrics for Bedrock

Most production problems can be diagnosed using specific signals in the AWS/Bedrock namespace in CloudWatch. The following table outlines the key metrics used to monitor latency, throttling, and cost:

Category Metric Description
Latency InvocationLatency Measures time from API call to response.
Latency TimeToFirstToken Time until the first token is generated.
Latency OutputTokenCount Total output tokens generated.
Latency OTPS Output tokens per second (derived metric).
Throttling InvocationThrottles Count of throttled requests.
Throttling EstimatedTPMQuotaUsage Estimated tokens per minute quota consumption, including cache write tokens and output burndown multipliers, across inference APIs.
Cost InputTokenCount Uncached input tokens.
Cost CacheReadInputTokenCount Input tokens read from cache (lower cost than uncached).
Cost CacheWriteInputTokenCount Input tokens written to cache (can have higher cost depending on model).
Cost OutputTokenCount Generated output tokens.

The EstimatedTPMQuotaUsage metric helps teams set proactive alarms, track quota consumption across models, and request quota increases before hitting rate limits. A lower cache hit rate can increase the cost per request due to the pricing differences between uncached input and cache reads.

💡 Why It Matters

In a period of about five weeks, eight new models were released. By mid-October, approximately two-thirds of engineer requests through coding agents were directed to these new models. Each release can simultaneously change output tokens, cost, latency, and capacity. Since published benchmark charts do not always reflect how a model handles specific internal workloads, Airbnb’s approach of running evals on their own tasks and monitoring distinct CloudWatch signals allows them to choose appropriate default models and reasoning effort ceilings for their engineers.

item.title: Event‑Driven Sync of MCP Server Tools to AWS Agent Registry
item.description:
Event‑Driven Sync of MCP Server Tools to AWS Agent Registry

When a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server published in the AWS Agent Registry gains a new tool or updates its schema, the registry record is automatically refreshed via an event‑driven workflow.

🔍 Overview

  • An MCP server published in the AWS Agent Registry must keep its tool or schema record up‑to‑date.
  • An event‑driven workflow uses AWS CloudTrail, Amazon EventBridge, and AWS Lambda to automate the update.
  • The solution works in both single‑account and multi‑account environments.

🏗️ Architecture

  • AWS CloudTrail – captures UpdateAgentRuntime API calls as management events.
  • Amazon EventBridge – routes matching events to a Lambda function; supports cross‑account forwarding.
  • AWS Lambda (sync function) – queries the MCP server, diffs the tool list against the registry, and updates the record when needed.
  • AWS Agent Registry – stores MCP server records and their tool schemas as the source of truth.
  • AgentCore Identity – brokers OAuth token exchanges so the Lambda can authenticate without storing secrets.
  • Account roles
    • Account A (registry account) owns the Agent Registry, EventBridge rule, sync Lambda, and CloudTrail logs.
    • Account B (MCP server account) hosts the MCP server runtime and the Amazon Cognito OAuth provider.

⚙️ How It Works

  1. A developer updates an MCP server in Account B; the server calls the UpdateAgentRuntime API (via AgentCore CLI or directly).
  2. CloudTrail in Account B records the call as a management event (≈ 5–15 min delay).
  3. EventBridge in Account B captures the CloudTrail event and forwards it to the default EventBridge bus in Account A (cross‑account rule when applicable).
  4. The EventBridge rule in Account A triggers the sync Lambda, passing the full CloudTrail event JSON.
  5. The Lambda extracts the runtime Amazon Resource Name (ARN) from the event and builds the MCP server’s invocation URL.
  6. The Lambda obtains a secure OAuth bearer token through AgentCore Identity.
  7. The Lambda calls the MCP server (initialize, then tools/list) to retrieve the latest tools information.
  8. The Lambda locates the corresponding registry record by ARN, compares the retrieved schema with the stored one, and updates the record if a change is detected.
  9. The process assumes the registry already contains a pre‑registered record for the MCP server; the Lambda updates existing records only and does not create new ones.

🚀 Availability

  • The same workflow runs unchanged in a single‑account deployment where the registry, Lambda, EventBridge rule, and MCP server all reside in Account A.
  • In a multi‑account deployment, runtime events flow securely from Account B to Account A before the Lambda performs the sync.

item.title: Circle K Deploys Automated Incident Triage Using Amazon Bedrock
item.description:
Circle K Deploys Automated Incident Triage Using Amazon Bedrock

This post was co‑written with Marek Klatowicz, Cloud DevOps Engineer at Circle K.

🔍 Overview

Circle K runs a cloud‑native infrastructure on AWS that powers point‑of‑sale systems, loyalty applications, and electric‑vehicle charging across more than 17,200 convenience and fuel retail stores in 27 countries. The DevOps team monitors this environment with Grafana and receives alerts for container restarts, error‑rate spikes, latency issues, and failed deployments.

⚠️ Manual Triage Pain

When an alert fires, engineers typically spend 45–60 minutes repeating the same steps:

  • Review recent logs in Amazon CloudWatch.
  • Examine application traces in Amazon OpenSearch Service.
  • Check Amazon ECS task status.
  • Cross‑reference symptoms with internal runbooks stored in GitHub. The depth and speed of triage vary with each on‑call engineer’s familiarity with the affected service.

🤖 Solution: Agentic AI Triage with Amazon Bedrock

Circle K built an automated triage system that uses Amazon Bedrock, a fully managed service that makes foundation models available through a single API. The system employs an agentic AI architecture that investigates each incident autonomously and delivers a structured summary to Slack within minutes of an alert firing.

Key Bedrock Benefits

  • Single API access to multiple foundation models; models can be swapped without code changes.
  • Native integration with existing AWS IAM, VPC, and logging configurations.
  • Built‑in orchestration that lets agents call AWS APIs, query databases, and retrieve documents.
  • Bedrock Knowledge Bases provide managed Retrieval‑Augmented Generation, handling ingestion and retrieval of internal product cards without a separate vector database.
  • Customer data is not shared with model providers nor used to train foundation models, satisfying Circle K’s security requirements.

🏗️ Architecture

The end‑to‑end flow starts with a Grafana alert and proceeds through AWS services as follows:

Component Role
Grafana alert Publishes a notification to Amazon SNS
Amazon SNS Forwards the notification to an Amazon SQS queue
Amazon SQS Holds the alert payload for processing
AWS Lambda Polls the queue, extracts the payload, and invokes an Amazon Bedrock Flow
Amazon Bedrock Flow Orchestrates two parallel agents that perform log queries, health checks, and runbook lookups
Slack Receives the structured incident summary

📊 Impact

Since deployment, Circle K’s mean triage time has dropped to under 15 minutes—a 67–75 percent reduction according to internal incident‑response metrics. On‑call engineers now receive actionable context instead of raw alerts, allowing immediate remediation.

🚀 Availability

Amazon Bedrock model availability varies by AWS Region; refer to the “Supported models by AWS Region” documentation for details.

💡 Why It Matters

  • Consistent, fast triage reduces mean time to resolution.
  • Reduces manual effort and reliance on individual engineer expertise.
  • Meets strict security requirements by keeping sensitive operational data within the customer’s AWS account.
  • Eliminates the overhead of self‑hosting foundation models, prompting, versioning, and tool orchestration.

item.title: CDK Construct Eliminates SageMaker Endpoint Update Failures with Auto Scaling
item.description:
CDK Construct Eliminates SageMaker Endpoint Update Failures with Auto Scaling

Updating an Amazon SageMaker AI real‑time endpoint configuration (changing instance type, count, or environment variables) through AWS CloudFormation or the AWS CDK can cause deployment failures.

🔍 Overview

  • CloudFormation tries to update the endpoint while the scalable target is still registered.
  • SageMaker blocks the endpoint update before CloudFormation reaches the auto‑scaling resources.
  • If the scalable target is deregistered manually via the AWS CLI, the deployment succeeds, but CloudFormation does not re‑register the auto‑scaling resources. The endpoint runs without scaling and no error is reported.
  • The stack’s rollback also fails (UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED), leaving the stack in a broken state that requires manual console intervention.

⚙️ How It Works

A reusable CDK construct replaces the native AWS::ApplicationAutoScaling::ScalableTarget and AWS::ApplicationAutoScaling::ScalingPolicy resources with three custom resources that orchestrate the deregister‑register cycle around the endpoint update.

Custom Resource Purpose
Deregister Removes the scalable target before the endpoint update begins.
Register Scalable Target Waits for the endpoint to reach InService status, then registers the scalable target.
Attach Scaling Policy Waits for the scalable target to be queryable, then applies the target‑tracking scaling policy.
  • The construct enforces explicit dependency ordering with node.add_dependency calls in CDK.
  • Each custom resource is backed by a Step Functions state machine and Lambda functions.
  • A ConfigHash property forces CloudFormation to re‑invoke the Lambda functions whenever a configuration value changes.

📦 Implementation Details

  • The deployed stack contains:
    • 3 custom resources (Deregister, Register Scalable Target, Attach Scaling Policy)
    • 2 Step Functions state machines
    • 12 Lambda functions
      • 5 functions are the construct’s own handlers (one for Deregister and an on_event/is_complete pair for each asynchronous resource).
      • 7 functions are generated by the CDK provider framework.
  • Provider total_timeout limits:
    • 1 hour for Register Scalable Target
    • 15 minutes for Attach Scaling Policy
  • You do not need to write or maintain the framework‑generated functions; they are included automatically.

✅ Benefits

  • Update endpoint configuration and auto‑scaling parameters in a single deployment without manual steps.
  • Eliminates the hidden failure where the endpoint runs without auto scaling and no error is shown.
  • Prevents UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED scenarios, keeping the CloudFormation stack healthy.
  • Provides deterministic ordering of deregister → endpoint update → register → attach policy.

item.title: AWS adds automated remediation workflow using Lambda Durable Functions, EventBridge, and Bedrock
item.description:
AWS adds automated remediation workflow using Lambda Durable Functions, EventBridge, and Bedrock

AWS announced an update that extends the AWS DevOps Agent with an automated remediation workflow built on AWS Lambda Durable Functions, Amazon EventBridge, and Amazon Bedrock. The new flow keeps the DevOps Agent in its safe observe‑and‑report mode while adding a controlled, programmable step that can apply fixes after a single approval.

🔍 Overview

  • Reducing the time between incident detection, investigation, and remediation is a critical priority for organizations running production workloads on AWS.
  • When an issue arises, on‑call engineers often need to diagnose the problem across components, identify the root cause, and apply a fix, sometimes in the middle of the night.
  • AWS DevOps Agent automatically triages incidents, provides root‑cause analysis (RCA) and recommended actions, but typically does not modify production resources directly.
  • The update demonstrates how to combine AWS Lambda Durable Functions, Amazon EventBridge, and Amazon Bedrock to automate the remediation step, turning investigation summaries into pre‑validated fixes ready for a single approval.

🧩 How it works

  1. Investigation completed – AWS DevOps Agent emits an event containing symptoms, findings, and RCA.
  2. Event receipt – Amazon EventBridge receives the investigation‑completion event and triggers the devops-agent-trigger Lambda function with the investigation content.
  3. Orchestration start – The trigger function packages the summary and starts the devops-agent-remediation-durable durable function.
  4. Bedrock analysis – The durable function sends the investigation context to Amazon Bedrock. Bedrock analyzes the findings and searches an allowlist of approved Lambda tools (e.g., devops-agent-lambda-tool).
  5. Tool selection – Bedrock proposes specific remediation actions based on the findings and the available tools.
  6. Read‑only execution – For read‑only actions, the durable function runs the selected tools autonomously.
  7. Mutating actions – For infrastructure‑changing actions, the workflow pauses and waits for a human approval signal.
  8. Approval & execution – After approval, the durable function applies the remediation actions using the selected tools.
  9. Iterative loop – The function operates as an agentic loop, repeatedly invoking Bedrock, executing approved tools, and feeding results back until remediation is complete.

⚙️ Key details

  • Lambda Durable Functions can run for up to one year without extra infrastructure, automatically checkpoint progress, suspend during long‑running tasks, and recover from failures.
  • The orchestrator enforces a curated allowlist of remediation tools; each tool is a purpose‑built Lambda function that performs a single, well‑scoped action (e.g., reading a Lambda configuration or updating an IAM policy statement).
  • Read‑only tools run autonomously; mutating tools cause the durable function to pause and wait for an approve/reject signal.
  • The approval signal accepts an arbitrary JSON payload, allowing parameter overrides or reviewer observations to be fed back into the Bedrock conversation before execution.
Tool (allowlist) Purpose
devops-agent-lambda-tool Performs a specific, well‑scoped action such as reading a Lambda configuration or updating an IAM policy statement

🚀 Benefits

  • Reduces mean time to resolution (MTTR) by preparing pre‑validated changes that require only a single approval click.
  • Frees on‑call engineers from repetitive diagnostic and manual remediation steps.
  • Keeps automated actions auditable and safe by limiting execution to an approved set of Lambda tools.
  • Allows the workflow to pause for minutes, hours, or days without consuming compute resources, then resume exactly where it left off.

📈 Real‑world impact – Cornerstone Orion AI

  • Cornerstone OnDemand’s Orion AI, built with Amazon Bedrock and Strands Agents, reduced database incident diagnosis time from 45 minutes to 10 minutes (a 78 % reduction).
  • A three‑person team delivered Orion AI in six months.
  • Orion AI also eliminated a 15‑minute reporting lag between SRE and data teams, reduced redundant alerts by a median of 65 %, and collapsed a four‑step manual handoff into a single interaction.
  • The system illustrates the same principles: AI‑driven investigation, curated tool execution, and human‑in‑the‑loop approval.

The updated workflow shows how AWS services can be combined to automate the full incident‑response loop while preserving control and auditability.

#AWS #DevOpsAgent #LambdaDurable #Bedrock #Automation

item.title: NVIDIA DSX Air Introduces Node‑Based Digital Twin for AI Factory Validation
item.description:
NVIDIA DSX Air Introduces Node‑Based Digital Twin for AI Factory Validation

AI factories are some of the most complex operations in the world, combining GPUs, CPUs, switches, DPUs, and SuperNICs alongside schedulers, orchestration services, security controls, and a rapidly changing software stack.

🔍 Overview

  • To minimize time to first token, AI factory operators can’t wait until hardware arrives before validating it.
  • NVIDIA DSX Air provides a digital twin for the AI factory: a simulation environment where teams can model, validate, and operate against an AI‑factory design throughout its lifecycle.

🧩 How it works

  • A node‑based digital twin simulation is a high‑fidelity, executable representation of an AI factory’s infrastructure and operational interfaces.
  • Unlike a physical replica, it gives platform teams a safe, API‑accessible environment in which to model the hardware topology and software stack, exercise change, observe behavior, and validate outcomes before a production change is made.
  • Integrated into the CI/CD pipeline, it can automatically validate supported configuration and software changes before promotion.
  • It extends simulation from a planning activity into a continuously available operational capability.
  • Agents can interrogate the twin, run checks, compare outcomes, retrieve relevant operational context, and initiate follow‑up workflows.
  • Its characteristics emerge from interactions across layers: accelerator configuration, network fabric, storage, Kubernetes and scheduling, GPU orchestration, tenant isolation, identity and access controls, observability, and the AI applications themselves.

⚙️ Key features

  • Traditional environments often force teams to wait for physical hardware to be racked and cabled, assemble a lab, perform software bring‑up, and then validate that the system is working as planned.
  • A node‑based digital twin represents supported infrastructure software and APIs, so teams can work against a representative environment before hardware availability or production deployment.
  • Teams can validate supported configuration and software changes in the logical twin before promoting them through the delivery pipeline.
  • Test representative, large‑scale designs and workflows before committing physical infrastructure or production capacity.
  • Test supported network configurations and software integrations in the twin before making production changes.
  • Use the same model across Day 0 planning, Day 1 deployment, and Day 2 operations.
  • The node‑based simulation as a logical digital twin is not intended to replace every simulation technique.
  • It becomes the high‑fidelity integration and validation layer within a broader simulation strategy.
  • Node‑based simulation supports integration testing and operational validation of supported configurations and software.
  • Separate cluster, performance, power, and memory models can inform capacity and resource planning within their validated scope.
  • A performance model can predict the effect of a configuration.
  • A node‑based simulation can show what happens when the intended stack, APIs, policies, and orchestrators execute together.

🚀 Agentic Automation & Governance

  • An agent can be assigned a bounded goal, use approved tools to query or change the digital twin, evaluate the resulting state, and return evidence‑backed recommendations or trigger a governed workflow.
  • The agent configures or selects the relevant logical twin, including topology, tenant policy, workload profile, and operational constraints.
  • The agent runs the validation tools available to the workflow, such as supported configuration checks, security and compliance checks, and infrastructure health analysis.
  • It compares results with organizational policy and domain knowledge retrieved from approved documentation.
  • It produces an evidence‑based report and either recommends promotion, opens a remediation task, or routes the case for human approval.
  • This is a governed automation model, not an invitation to give agents unconstrained production access.
  • The simulation platform provides the sandbox where agents can explore, test, and propose change.
  • Human‑in‑the‑loop gates and policy controls determine when a result can affect production.

💡 Why it matters

  • The standard way companies justify automation investments, hours saved times labor cost minus build cost, was designed for rule‑based tools like robotic process automation (RPA).
  • That model misses most of the value agents create.
  • The classic return on investment (ROI) model was built for stable, high‑volume, rule‑based work: count the transactions, measure the minutes, multiply by a loaded rate, subtract the build cost.
  • RPA earned its place on those terms.
  • It assumes processes are stable, so it ignores the cost of maintaining automation as they change.
  • It assumes tasks are rule‑based, so it has no line item for exceptions.
  • It assumes the work is the whole job, so it never counts the cost of human oversight.
  • And it treats a saved hour as banked value, when freed capacity often refills with backlog and never reaches the profit and loss statement (P&L).
  • Underfunding the work that turns saved hours into results is the mistake McKinsey says companies keep making: successful AI transformations follow a “1:3:5 pattern,” where “for every dollar invested in agentic technology, organizations spend three on process redesign and five on capability building and adoption.” However, most companies invert this formula entirely” (McKinsey, “Agentic AI change management: Closing the adoption gap,” 2026).
  • We assume the value of automation lives in the task, but in agentic automation most of it lives around the task: the judgment, the exceptions, the coordination across systems.
  • The real gains come from redesigning the workflow around agents, not from dropping an agent into an unchanged process.
  • A better business case measures four dimensions of value, plus the condition that determines whether they reach the P&L. We call it the Agentic Value Model.
  • AWS guidance gives planning ranges: correcting an error can cost 1.5–4 times the original transaction, and human error can account for 2–15 percent of operational cost (AWS Prescriptive Guidance, “Assessing your current human‑process costs”).
  • As AWS notes, “low‑volume, high‑value decisions might justify agentic assistance for improved decision quality rather than cost reduction” (AWS Prescriptive Guidance, “Understanding agentic AI economics”).

#AIFactory #DigitalTwin #AgenticAutomation #CI/CD

item.title: NVIDIA AI Cluster Runtime v1.0 delivers version‑locked GPU‑Kubernetes recipes
item.description:
NVIDIA AI Cluster Runtime v1.0 delivers version‑locked GPU‑Kubernetes recipes

NVIDIA released version 1.0 of the AI Cluster Runtime (AICR), a library of version‑locked, validated recipes that simplify the configuration of GPU‑accelerated Kubernetes clusters.

🔍 Overview

  • GPU‑accelerated Kubernetes clusters depend on compatible versions across dozens of components, each on its own release cycle: host kernels, GPU drivers, container runtimes, networking, storage, operators, and workload frameworks.
  • A configuration that works for one service, GPU generation, and Kubernetes release may silently fail for another, and tracing version conflicts after deployment is slow and error‑prone.
  • AICR addresses this with version‑locked, validated recipes for GPU cluster configuration.

🧩 How it works

AICR element Purpose
Recipe Describes the desired, version‑locked component configuration and the constraints and validation phases that apply to it.
Bundle Renders the recipe into deployment artifacts for Helm, Argo CD, Flux, or Helmfile (or other IaC tools).
Snapshot Records observed cluster state, including Kubernetes, operating system, kernel, GPU, and topology information.
Validation Compares the recipe with observed state and, where declared, runs deployment, conformance, and performance checks; records signed evidence of the result.

The workflow is:

  1. Operator selects criteria (e.g., service, GPU, OS, workload intent) on the validation dashboard.
  2. The dashboard resolves those criteria to a pinned recipe.
  3. The recipe is rendered as a bundle for the operator’s preferred deployment tool (Argo CD, Helm, Flux, Helmfile, etc.).
  4. The bundle is applied to the cluster using the chosen CD tool.
  5. AICR validates the running cluster against the same recipe and stores signed evidence.

⚙️ Key details

  • All recipes are version‑locked and carry signed validation evidence from the hardware they were tested on.
  • v1.0 establishes a stable compatibility contract across its CLI, REST API, Go SDK, bundle layout, and artifact schemas.
  • The v1.x compatibility policy allows integrators to build against AICR’s public interfaces.
  • Contributors can propose recipes, validate them on their own clusters, and submit signed evidence for maintainer review.
  • Recent additions include live‑cluster validation, signed evidence, public evidence aggregation, and supply‑chain verification.
  • Merge‑blocking checks and committed compatibility baselines protect the public integration surfaces.
  • Pulumi Labs exposes AICR through an infrastructure‑as‑code provider, while Mirantis’s k0rdent integration packages it for multi‑cluster management.
  • Together they demonstrate the value of defining GPU‑accelerated Kubernetes configuration once and consuming it through different tools.

🚀 Availability

  • v1.0 is the first stable release of AICR.
  • Over the past six months the library grew from a handful of recipes to a collection spanning major Kubernetes services and the current NVIDIA accelerator portfolio, rendered as deployer‑neutral bundles.
  • AICR now has over 100 distinct contributors, with almost half from outside of NVIDIA.

💡 Why it matters

  • Prevents silent failures caused by hidden version mismatches across components.
  • Centralises knowledge of working component combinations that previously lived in separate validation systems, deployment scripts, and runbooks.
  • Enables teams to discover, reproduce, and update working configurations through a single dashboard and a unified set of public interfaces.
  • Provides signed evidence and supply‑chain verification, increasing trust in the deployed cluster configuration.
  • Allows operators to keep their existing GitOps or IaC workflows (Helm, Argo CD, Flux, Helmfile) while guaranteeing the intended configuration does not change across tooling.

#NVIDIA #Kubernetes #GPU #AICR

Source: AICR v1.0: Open, stable, and verifiable GPU cluster configuration | NVIDIA Technical Blog

item.description:
SageMaker HyperPod integrates with Unified Studio and adds Spaces for governed GPU workloads

Amazon SageMaker HyperPod gives machine learning (ML) teams access to large pools of accelerated compute for training and fine‑tuning models. When several teams share a single cluster the technical setup is straightforward, but governance becomes the challenging part.

🔍 Overview

  • SageMaker HyperPod is a capability of Amazon SageMaker AI that provides purpose‑built infrastructure for foundation model training and inference at scale.
  • SageMaker Unified Studio is the data and AI development environment where teams build with their data and tools.
  • Unified Studio can connect a HyperPod cluster to a project, letting team members launch workloads, review cluster and task information, and open a JupyterLab workflow.
  • The integration keeps cluster management in SageMaker AI interfaces and APIs, allowing infrastructure teams to use established cloud‑operations processes while presenting approved compute to ML teams in their project context.

⚙️ Governance Model

  • Governance decisions include:
    • Which teams may use the cluster.
    • How much capacity each team receives.
    • How to handle competition for resources.
    • Who is accountable when usage drifts from policy.
  • When multiple teams share visibility into the same cluster, controls that govern who can do what become even more important.
  • A well‑governed environment separates:
    • Organizational administration
    • Project access
    • Cluster operations
    • Workload execution
  • Each layer answers a different question and uses different controls.

🏗️ Four Layers of Control

  1. Organization layer – identity and capacity policies that apply across the entire account.
  2. Project layer – collaboration boundaries defined in SageMaker Unified Studio (not strong runtime security boundaries).
  3. Cluster layer – AWS IAM, Amazon EKS, and Slurm controls that govern cluster‑level access.
  4. Workload layer – workload identity, data and KMS key policies, network policy, task‑view restrictions, and scheduler policy.

“A SageMaker HyperPod connection adds an approved cluster to a project. It doesn’t replace the cluster’s AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM), Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS), or Slurm controls.”

All four layers must be aligned before the cluster is made available.

🧩 SageMaker Spaces on HyperPod

  • Earlier this year Amazon launched SageMaker Spaces for HyperPod, an add‑on that lets developers create interactive development environments directly on HyperPod EKS clusters.
  • Benefits:
    • Run JupyterLab or Code Editor environments without leaving the browser or using CLI tools.
    • Reduce time from cluster access to productive development to a few clicks.
    • Run interactive workloads alongside training jobs and model deployment, with support for fractional GPU allocations.
  • Management UI:
    • The new IDE and Notebooks tab on the HyperPod cluster detail page provides a complete user interface for Space management, removing the need for daily CLI commands.
    • Create Spaces with configurable compute, namespaces, storage, and HyperPod Task Governance for compute‑quota management via a guided form.
    • View all Spaces in a searchable table showing name, application type, status, access type, storage, GPU, and vCPU allocations.
    • Start or stop Spaces with a single selection to free compute when not in use.
    • Open Spaces directly in the browser (JupyterLab or Code Editor) or connect through a remote IDE such as VS Code.

🚀 Installing and Using Spaces

  1. Install the Spaces add‑on on the HyperPod EKS cluster from the SageMaker AI console → IDE and Notebooks tab. Choose Quick install (one‑click defaults) or Custom install (required for web UI access).
  2. Configure EKS access entries by attaching the managed policies:
    • AmazonSagemakerHyperpodSpacePolicy
    • AmazonSagemakerHyperpodUserClusterPolicy
    • AmazonSagemakerHyperpodSpaceTemplatePolicy to the IAM roles used by data scientists.
  3. Enable per‑user identity propagation on the Studio domain if it existed before the integration. This ensures each Studio user’s actions on the cluster are attributed in EKS access entries and AWS CloudTrail, enforcing strict Space ownership.
  4. Create and launch a Space:
    • In Studio, go to Compute → HyperPod, select the IDE and Notebooks tab.
    • After the Space status shows Running (a few minutes on a cold cluster, ~30–40 seconds with over‑provisioning), click Open to launch JupyterLab or Code Editor, or Open in VS Code for a remote IDE experience.

📚 Summary

  • By connecting SageMaker HyperPod clusters to Unified Studio projects, organizations can provide approved, high‑performance GPU compute to ML teams while retaining strong governance through four layered controls.
  • The new SageMaker Spaces UI gives data scientists a visual, click‑based workflow to create, manage, and use interactive development environments on the same HyperPod infrastructure that powers large‑scale training and inference.
  • This combination delivers a repeatable, governed model that separates infrastructure operations from project‑level development, enabling efficient use of shared GPU resources.

#SageMaker #HyperPod #MLOps #AIInfrastructure #MachineLearning

item.title: AWS Cloud Development Kit Enables Infrastructure Definition Using Modern Programming Languages
item.description:
AWS Cloud Development Kit Enables Infrastructure Definition Using Modern Programming Languages

The AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) is an open-source software development framework designed to define cloud infrastructure in code and provision it through AWS CloudFormation. It offers high-level object-oriented abstractions to define AWS resources imperatively using several modern programming languages.

🔍 Overview

The CDK allows developers to encapsulate AWS best practices within infrastructure definitions using a library of infrastructure constructs. This approach aims to reduce the complexity and glue-logic typically required when integrating various AWS services. By using the framework, developers can share infrastructure definitions without managing boilerplate logic.

🧩 How it works

Developers use the CDK framework in one of the supported programming languages to build components through a specific hierarchy:

  • Constructs: Reusable cloud components that encapsulate the details of how to use AWS.
  • Stacks: Compositions of constructs grouped together.
  • CDK App: The final application formed by one or more stacks.

Developers interact with their applications using the AWS CDK CLI. The CLI allows for the synthesis of artifacts such as AWS CloudFormation Templates, the deployment of stacks to development AWS accounts, and the ability to “diff” against a deployed stack to understand the impact of code changes.

⚙️ Key details

The AWS Construct Library includes modules for each AWS service. These modules are assigned stability designations that determine how they are updated:

Stability Designation Versioning Policy
Experimental Modules currently being built; may have breaking API changes in any release.
Stable Adheres to semantic versioning; breaking changes can only occur in major releases.

🚀 Availability

The AWS CDK is available for several programming languages with specific environment requirements:

Language Requirements
JavaScript / TypeScript Node.js >= 20.x
Python Python >= 3.8
Java Java >= 8 and Maven >= 3.5.4
.NET .NET >= 8.0
Go Go >= 1.16.4

Third-party language versions are supported until their vendor or community End Of Life (EOL). The AWS CDK CLI can be installed or updated via npm and requires Node.js >= 14.15.0, though using a version in Active LTS is recommended.

item.title: Four‑Agent AI Pattern Cuts Migration IaC Time from Weeks to Minutes
item.description:
Four‑Agent AI Pattern Cuts Migration IaC Time from Weeks to Minutes

🔍 Overview

The four‑agent pattern introduced by AWS Professional Services adds purpose‑built AI agents to an existing AWS Transform migration program. By attaching to AWS Transform, AWS Database Migration Service (DMS), and Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools, the pattern reduces infrastructure‑as‑code (IaC) generation from three‑to‑four weeks per application to minutes.

🧩 How it works

  • Hybrid integration – The agents run alongside AWS Transform (migration and modernization) and AWS DMS (database tier) rather than replacing them.
  • MCP‑connected sources – Agents access migration inputs and output destinations through MCP tools that each organization builds and maintains (e.g., internal wiki with security standards, ticketing system, collaboration platform, in‑house provisioning API).
  • Security at every touchpoint – The architecture applies security when reading inputs, generating IaC, and operating after cutover.
  • Serverless hosting – All agents are hosted in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime, which provides container‑based execution, session isolation, and multi‑agent orchestration.

Command Description
openhands Launch interactive terminal UI
openhands --headless -t "task" Run in headless mode for CI/CD, scripts, automation
openhands web Open browser‑based TUI

openhands --always-approve (or --yolo) Auto‑approve all actions

item.title: AI CLI Tooling Shifts Focus From Model Capability to Orchestration Reliability and Session Integrity
item.description:
AI CLI Tooling Shifts Focus From Model Capability to Orchestration Reliability and Session Integrity

The AI CLI tooling landscape has consolidated around seven major products representing corporate giants like Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, and GitHub/Alibaba alongside independent developers such as OpenCode and earandil-works. Recent developments indicate a market shift where competition now centers on agent orchestration reliability, session integrity, cost transparency, and enterprise manageability rather than core code-generation capability. Technical issues are increasingly focused on harness failures rather than model quality, with communities demanding auditable spend and replayable transcripts.

🔍 Overview

Performance metrics for the current landscape show distinct operational styles among the leading tools. While most tools are maturing, systemic weak points remain, specifically regarding cross-platform gaps on Windows and multi-provider routing (BYOK).

Tool Key Engagement & Operational Status
OpenAI Codex Highest absolute engagement and PR throughput; 50 automated internal merges via copyberry[bot].
Pi Highest velocity relative to project size (50 issues/30 PRs touched).
Qwen Code Most structured release engineering including stable, nightly, and vendored binaries.
Copilot CLI Zero PR movement recorded despite shipping a new release.

⚙️ Key Details

Reliability and observability have become primary development targets for Gemini CLI, Claude Code, Codex, Qwen Code, and OpenCode. Current issue queues highlight specific orchestration failures:

  • Agent Reliability: Gemini reported subagents claiming success after reaching maximum turns, while Claude Code encountered hidden mid-turn messages and orphaned subprocesses.
  • Security Standards: Claude Code and Qwen Code both faced shell-permission parsing bugs related to how separators like “;” and “&&” are handled, signaling a need for a shared command-parsing standard.
  • Cost Transparency: Users are pushing for better accounting, citing issues such as Pi’s cache-TTL billing bugs and Codex’s 5h-window usage exhaustion.
  • Enterprise Policy: Focus has increased on governance, such as Claude Code’s sandbox rule semantics and Codex’s Identity Provider-aware MCP catalog.

🧩 Universal Pain Points

Session persistence and resume integrity represent the most universal pain points across all seven tools. Specific regressions include silent data loss in Claude Code, stale connection IDs in Copilot CLI, and corrupted base64 or orphaned tool calls in Pi.

Windows compatibility remains a significant hurdle. Codex has approximately half of its top-15 queue dedicated to Windows-specific issues like lsass leaks and AppX problems. Other tools report PowerShell stalls, Defender false positives, and EPERM errors during extension renames on NTFS systems.

🚀 Availability

Recent releases and version updates across the ecosystem include:

  • Claude Code: v2.1.271 (Stable)
  • Gemini CLI: 2 alphas (0.155.0-alpha.4 / -alpha.2.4)
  • Qwen Code: v0.61.0 (Nightly)
  • Pi: v1.0.84-7 (2 consecutive patches)
  • Copilot CLI: v1.18.31 (Bugfix)
  • OpenCode: v0.23.4 (Stable) and 4 CUA driver binaries

💡 Why it Matters

The industry is moving toward remote and headless operations. Codex is investing in a Rust core with mobile remote control capabilities, while Qwen is developing a normative daemon protocol and remote web shells. These advancements, paired with new frameworks like the Claude Code Mods framework, suggest a transition from simple CLI wrappers to complex, verifiable agent platforms.

🚀 Building Enterprise Patching and Inventory Dashboards Using Amazon QuickSight

Architecture diagram for the enterprise patching and inventory dashboard solution

In today’s fast-paced IT environment, monitoring and visualizing patching compliance across your infrastructure is crucial. This comprehensive guide explores how Amazon QuickSight transforms the traditional manual dashboard creation process through AI-powered natural language interactions, enabling you to quickly generate insightful patching compliance and inventory visualizations.

💡 Solution Overview

The solution leverages several AWS services to automate the creation of Amazon QuickSight datasets and utilize natural language queries to visualize data. This innovative approach reduces what was once a multi-step manual process into a few simple prompts, saving valuable time while maintaining accuracy and providing real-time insights into your organization’s patching status.

🏗️ Architecture Component

The solution operates through the following key components:

  • AWS Systems Manager (SSM) - Executes custom scripts to gather inventory information
  • Amazon S3 - Central storage for inventory and patching data
  • AWS Glue - Data cataloging and crawling services
  • Amazon Athena - Query engine for data analysis
  • Amazon QuickSight - AI-powered visualization and dashboard creation
  • AWS CloudFormation - Infrastructure-as-code deployment

⚙️ Key Features

Infrastructure Insights Collected:

  • Cloud provider information (AWS, on-premises VMware, etc.)
  • Total and free disk space with status monitoring
  • Disk space percentage and critical alerts
  • EC2-specific metadata including hypervisor types, instance types, and driver versions

Automated Scheduling:

  • Systems Manager Association: Custom inventory collection every 7 days
  • AWS Glue Crawler: Data synchronization every 12 hours
  • Both intervals are customizable based on organizational requirements

📋 Prerequisites

Before implementing this solution, ensure you have:

  • ✅ Systems Manager Managed nodes (EC2 instances or hybrid nodes)
  • ✅ Systems Manager Inventory enabled on target accounts
  • ✅ Systems Manager patch scan/install operations configured
  • ✅ Amazon QuickSight user account with Admin Pro or Author Pro privileges
  • ✅ CloudFormation StackSets permissions
  • ✅ AWS Organization ID (if using Organizations)

🔧 Implementation Walkthrough

Step 1: Deploy the CloudFormation Stack

  1. Download the CloudFormation template from the GitHub repository 2. Configure deployment parameters:
Parameter Category Key Parameters Description
SSM Configuration S3 Bucket Name Central bucket for resource data sync
Target Type ALL instances, TAG-based, or specific targeting

QuickSight User QuickSight username for permissions

Step 2: Configure QuickSight Permissions

  1. Navigate to Amazon QuickSight console 2. Set user role to Admin Pro:

    • Choose user icon → Manage QuickSight - Select Manage users → Assign Admin Pro role

  2. Configure AWS resource access: - Under Permissions → AWS resources

    • Enable Amazon Athena and Amazon S3 access - Select the S3 bucket created by CloudFormation

Step 3: Initialize Data Collection

  1. Wait for SSM Inventory Association to complete (runs every 30 minutes) 2. Manually trigger AWS Glue Crawler:
    • Navigate to AWS Glue Crawlers console - Select crawler starting with “SSM-GlueCrawler-*”
    • Choose Run to execute

🎯 Interactive Querying

Example queries:

  • “List of resourceid by diskspacestatus equal Critical”

This solution demonstrates how Amazon QuickSight’s AI capabilities transform infrastructure monitoring from a complex, time-intensive process into an intuitive, natural language-driven experience.   • Accelerate dashboard creation from hours to minutes
